utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is the case IT-03-69-T, The Prosecutor versus Jovica Stanisic and Franko Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There was one matter still pending since last Friday; that's the Prosecution motion for leave to reply to the Defence response to the 18th Prosecution motion for leave to amend its 65 ter exhibit list. What I think, Mr. Jordash, you indicated that you would give your position on that matter today, leave to reply.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We don't -- we don't oppose the application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As well, likewise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Leave is therefore granted, Mr. Groome. Prosecution reply to be filed by Friday, the 5th of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Jordash.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: We also don't oppose the application for leave to reply to the Defence responsible to the bar table motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, same position as far as you're concerned?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Same, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Groome, any idea on how much time you would need to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I don't, Your Honour. But I could have that information by the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could please tell us after the first break, then we will rule on the matter. Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that last Friday at ten minutes past 7.00 I again - which is not what I'm used to do - have forgotten to instruct you not to speak with anyone about your testimony. But being -- well, rather familiar with the practice and having been here for a couple of days, may I take it that you have not discussed your testimony with anyone?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then, Mr. Jordash, since you had given up your one-minute question, it's now for Mr. Bakrac to ... we discussed that you had one question on the basis of a document which you disclosed rather late, and later you said, No, I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Yes, that's -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I leave that. So that means that Mr. Bakrac is now the one who is ready to cross-examine the witness. Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Theunens, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Bakrac is counsel for Mr. Simatovic. And I again instruct you, before I forget that as well, that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you have given at the beginning of your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Good afternoon to all in the courtroom, in and around the courtroom. Mr. Theunens, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I would like to start my cross-examination in relation to your report by dealing with some documents or, rather, the Law on All People's Defence, and I believe that that is where you had started from as well, in your report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So could we please have P1010 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the document, Mr. Theunens, I would like to draw your attention -- no. No, actually, first I'm going to ask you whether it's correct that this Law on All People's Defence of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia that was passed on the 23rd of April, 1982 -- or, rather, that is when it was published in the Official Gazette in 1982, whether it was in force until the Law on Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was passed in 1994?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If your question refers to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, as it was established in May 1992, then the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Could we now have a look at Article 13. However, it seems that we did not understand each other. We're waiting for Article 13 to appear on our screens, but my question was whether the Law on All People's Defence from 1982 was in force all the way up until 1994 when the Law on Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was passed.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to explain my answer that the 1982 law applied to all republics of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, i.e., all six. Of course, the 1994 law only applies to the two republics that constituted FRY, i.e., Serbia and Montenegro. And the other four republics became independent before May 1992, so that's why I tried to be specific and explain that the 1982 law only became -- only remained invalid for Serbia and Montenegro, i.e., FRY, until the adoption the 1994 FRY law.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens, now it is much clearer. So please do have a look at Article 13. I would like for us to interpret it together. Actually, I'm asking you how it is that you understand this joint provision of Article 13. It says here that: "Working people and citizens have the right and duty to organise themselves and take part in the organisation, preparation for and implementation of All People's Defence; to educate or train for All People's Defence; and for carrying out tasks in times of war in the convenient of an immediate threat of war or other emergencies; to take part in armed struggle and other forms of All People's resistance in order to protect and rescue citizens and material goods from wartime devastation and other threats; and to carry out other tasks of interest for the defence of the country and the protection of the social order established by the SFRY constitution." So my question is: The Serb people, in Croatia and in Bosnia, who, at that point in time, in 1990 and 1991, were within the SFRY, would they have had the right to organise themselves on the basis of this article and to prepare for defence, for the defence of the state that they considered to be their own?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that this falls outside the scope of my report because it's essentially a legal question. However, I would just like to draw your attention to the reference in the article that these kind of activities, i.e., to defend the country, it is specified that one of the three states has to be declared: state of war, state of imminent threat of war, or I think that it's -- also mention is made of a state of emergency. And this is a decision which is taken by the highest political authority, i.e., the SFRY Presidency. So my understanding would be, from this article, that, indeed, they can participate in these activities if one of these three states has been declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right. Let's do it this way, Mr. Theunens. Shall we agree first on a fact that I believe should be beyond dispute; namely, that on the 3rd of October, 1991, a state of imminent threat of war had been declared?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But, I mean, not to be difficult, but there is some dispute in a sense that - and I have quoted it in my report - that one, I think, it's a minute of the meeting states that the state of imminent threat of war has been established. And it doesn't use the word "declared." However, a document from the, I think, the SSNO that follows this establishment refers to a declaration of the state of imminent threat of war, by the SFRY Presidency or what remains, at that stage, of the SFRY Presidency. And that should be in the beginning of part 2 of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we won't deal with that any longer. You said what you had to say in relation to that. I'm interested in the third situation. In the B/C/S version, this is what it reads verbatim: "Or other emergencies." When we say "or other emergencies," you're a military expert, an expert in military affair, hotbeds of crisis and so on, the arming of a political party like the HDZ was in a republic and preparation for cessation, could that be considered as one of these "other emergencies"?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have not analysed in this report the -- I mean, the matter raised by the Defence -- by Defence counsel. I mean, the arming by the HDZ and the preparation of cessation -- or cessation, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Theunens. I don't have time to dwell on this. That will do. So now please look at Article 64 from the same law. The last paragraph at that. I'm going to read the last paragraph out to you very slowly and I'm going to have a few questions in relation to that. "Socio-political and other social organisations and associations of citizens in accordance with their role and tasks develop and encourage various activities in preparing, organising, training, and the participation of their members and other working people and citizens in All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection and in carrying out other tasks of importance for the strengthening of the defence and self-protection capacity of the social community." So my first question would be: How do you interpret this? What are social political organisations, what are social organisations, and what are associations of citizens?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this refers to the concept of All People's Defence as it existed in the SFRY, whereby the entire population would participate in an organised manner in the defence of the country. One of the components of the defence consisted of the armed forces, whereby the armed forces were made up of the JNA and the TO. Now there could be also other participants in this All People's Defence like, for example, civil defence. I believe that also state-owned factories could participate. I mean, the people working there who didn't serve in the JNA or the TO could participate in the defence effort. But obviously the emphasis was on an organised structure -- on organised structures which would operate under -- under state control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. I would like to deal with these legal provisions very quickly. Let us look at Article 81 now, and I'll have two questions in relation to that. First paragraph of Article 81. So, Mr. Theunens, please look at Article 81 that says: "The Federal Secretariat for National Defence and certain commands, units, and institutions of the Yugoslav People's Army in cooperation with appropriate organs of socio-political communities ..." I would like to stop at this point and I would like to ask you, for example, can we interpret it this way: The MUP of a republic or the MUP of a municipality, can it be considered an appropriate organ of a socio-political community, an organ that is in charge?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I don't think I'm able to answer the question. I know that in Article 104 the police is identified as police in the -- in the All People's Defence law and not as a socio-political community or socio-political organisation. So I prefer not to answer, instead of trying to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I don't want to insist on something that you obviously haven't gone into in great detail. I'm just suggesting to you that a socio-political community is, say, a republic. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That may be correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can we agree that an appropriate organ, an organ in charge of that socio-political community or that republic, is the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Let us proceed. So these organs of socio-political communities, according to this law of the SFRY, have the right to provide professional assistance to self-management organisations and communities, socio-political and other social organisations, in preparing All People's Defence, notably regarding the preparation organisation of Territorial Defence, civil protection, and a system of monitoring and reporting. So according to this law, for instance, could the MUP give professional assistance, for instance, in monitoring and reporting, in procuring equipment, like radios, uniforms, and so on, in your view?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, yeah. If this assistance would be provided by the entities identified in the Article, I don't see a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. I don't want to go into an in-depth discussion. I want to deal with this to the degree to which you have dealt with these matters. And that is what is relevant to our Defence, and that is why I'm moving so quickly. Let us look at Article 94 now. This is a chapter that has to do with the armed forces, and the heading is: "Joint provisions." The subheading, rather. It is very brief. Please look at the text. "For the organisation and preparation of the armed forces within the rights and responsibilities established in the constitution and law, it is the socio-political communities, basic and other, organisations of associated labour and local communities that shall be responsible." So does this pertain to the same thing that you talked about, that even a local commune had a right to prepare for armed resistance, in one of those three aforementioned cases?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, if this is a -- these kind of activities are conducted in accordance with the overall legislation, and, for example, this is an reference here at the end of Article 94 in compliance with the social role and nature of the tasks, there -- there should not be a problem. And when I mean the overall legislation, I refer to the 1974 SFRY constitution and the 1982 Law on All People's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Can we now move on to a different document. And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... just for me to verify whether -- apparently the point you're making is that under this law the MUP of Serbia - and you referred to the MUP, you never referred to a MUP of a republic - was in a position to -- to assist in this self-defence which is organised by any of the organisations mentioned in this law. Have I understood that well?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. This was possible under the law. We will see what happened. But the point I'm trying to make is that this was permissible under the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and I see that point. So I, therefore, well understood your line of questioning. Are you also making the point that, therefore, the MUP of Croatia could have assisted organisations falling in the scope of this law in order to organise themselves against developments in other republics, because you're asking whether the MUP -- at least that was your point, that the MUP of Serbia had a right -- was in a position to -- to assist. Would that be true for the MUPs of all the republics, even if they would go against developments in the other republics? Is that included in the point you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do believe that this -- they would be included, because we're talking about the rights of the peoples to organise themselves and protect themselves, being threatened. Second, I'm not trying to testify here, but let us note that this is the SFRY constitution that one or two republics wanted to crush. Whereas, one constitutional entity within these republics wanted to preserve it. And under the -- the legislation, they had the right to defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I got your point. I might still be struggling with the end of Article 2 which says that -- after having listed again all these organisations: "... shall ensure that the preparation and implementation of All People's Defence and Social Self-Protection constitute a unique whole." But I'm still -- then would be struggling with that, but at least I got your point. And that is what I wanted to verify. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Can we have P1042, which is the Law on Defence of the Republic of Serbia. Let us look at Article 10, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: This is a law from 1991 which applies to the Republic of Serbia only, while the FRY was still in existence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us look at Article 10, which reads -- it's on page 2. It reads that: "The Ministry of Internal Affairs shall organise and implement defence preparations and its functioning in the case of an imminent threat of war or war. "Establish the organisation and the headcount of the police force in the event of an imminent threat of war or war." We spoke of the proclamation of the state of an imminent threat of war into October, so under the law, did the MUP have the right to organize and carry out preparations for defence and war?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood the question now because I thought you asked about Ministry of Interior and then in the transcript there is a reference to the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I may have misspoken. No, my question had to do with the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed. As is specified in the Article, okay, one of the three states has to be declared. And just to also refer to the point made by Your Honours, the uniqueness, as is referred to in -- in the Article of the All People's Defence law, refers to the principles of command and control that are defined in Article 112 of the 1982 All People's Defence law, page 29, part 1 of the report, where unity of command is one of the three principle, i.e., it's part -- all defence efforts have to be part of one bigger or one big effort and -- and all these smaller efforts that are part of it have to be coherent and consistent with the overall goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Let me follow up with the -- with this. When you say "unity of command," who is it who enforces unity of command under the law?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it starts at the level of the Supreme Command, which is a political body; and then as far as for the military is concerned, it goes down through the chain of command to the smallest unit. I mean, when I go from the top to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Let us look at another Article from this law; namely, Article 119, which is on page 45 in the B/C/S version. It is a short article as well. And I'd like to see what your understanding of the article is. Let me start reading slowly before we have it. Article 119 reads: "In the event that the interests of the Republic of Serbia as a state are under threat, as well as those of the Serbian People, the provisions of federal laws from the field of national defence shall apply as appropriate until such time as the republican laws are passed." So what I'd like to know is this: Does this Article provide for the application of, under the republican Serbian law, the Law on All People's Defence dating back to 1982, in those circumstances as well?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've seen this article before and I know there has been debate over it, but I have not been able to fully understand the last sentence, whether it means that Serbian law has priority over federal law or whether federal law has priority over Serbian law until Serbian law has been made coherent with federal law. So that's why also I haven't included this article in my report, and I don't -- I'm not qualified to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I also have some difficulties in understanding what Article 119 exactly means. And I wonder whether there's any translation problem, but perhaps I should ask the native speakers whether they can make any logic sense out of Article 119, in English. Perhaps I'm -- looking at Mr. Groome, looking at Mr. Jordash. So equally looking at both parties. Mr. Jordash, do you fully understand what Article 119 actually says?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: I think I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let me ask. Mr. Groome, do you also have no difficulties in understanding the language of Article 119?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I do have some difficulty. I'm just studying it now. Maybe Mr. -- Mr. ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- Weber ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm just reiterating what Mr. Groome just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... so there's one party who claims that he understands, being a native speaking person. Mr. Jordash, could you rephrase Article 119 in such a way that it becomes clear to us as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: The federal laws -- in a situation where the Republic of Serbia or its people's interests are endangered, the federal laws will apply until --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: -- the republican laws are passed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was struggling with the "as long as."

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Until.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Until. You understand "as long as" to be "until." Then, I must say, I have far less problems. Is that your understanding as well, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes. And perhaps my next question and reference to the 1994 FRY law will serve to clarify the matter. So I'll call up the 65 ter number of the federal law, because it was uploaded erroneously as a P exhibit. We only have the first page in English. So can we call up 65 ter 4418 and look at page 2, where two articles are listed -- or, rather, my apologies. Let us first look at the last page of the transitional and final provision, which is Article 87. It is a rather longish article, so I'll read it out for you: On the date of coming into effect of this law, the Law on All People's Defence, SFRY Official Gazette 81/17 and 31/91, will cease to exist -- will cease to -- will become null and void.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have the article so that we can follow what has just been read.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies, Your Honour. I didn't notice it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were reading from 87, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... The Registrar informs me that a translation of 87 is not uploaded in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe it was an error on my part. I relied on the Prosecution documents being uploaded. I did say that only page 1 was translated. I didn't look at the end of it. I didn't think it was going to be a problem. Even Mr. Theunens confirmed at the start of my cross-examination that the 1982 law was in force until 1994, when the Law on Defence of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can ask Mr. Theunens if he agrees with what I've just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me first re-read what you just read so that we have at least -- one second, please. Well, let me ... first of all, I have a problem with the server connection. Do I understand that Rule 87 is a kind of transitional rule which refers to all other kinds of other legislation and that you say that it [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Overlapping speakers] ... yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make it easier for you, I can read it out. It's just a sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you read out the one relevant sentence, that would assist.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's precisely what I wanted to do, Your Honour. Thank you. "On the date of the coming into force of the present law, the Law on All People's Defence (SFRY Official Gazette 21/82 and 35/92) will become null and void."

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Is that something you agreed with at the start of my cross-examination when I asked you whether this 1982 law was in force in the FRY until 1994?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, my -- it was indeed my reply that it was my understanding that the 1982 was still in force in FRY prior to the adoption of the FRY Law on Defence. And there's obviously a contradiction between what he's stated in Article 87 and, for example, the SFRY Presidency order number 73 from December 1991; it's the order on the engagement of volunteers in the armed forces of the SFRY during immediate danger of war. There -- I mean, this is from December, i.e., after the adoption of the Law on Defence of the Republic of Serbia. And in that order there is a clear reference to the Law on All People's Defence, so suggesting or indicating or even confirming that the Law on Defence is still valid. Now, I know - and, again, I'm not going go into legal analysis - but I know that the Law on Defence of the Republic of Serbia, as it was adopt in August 1991, as well as, I mean, in particular also Article 119 that was discussed, which basically states that for Serbia its own legislation has priority over federal legislation - here the defence law - that there was a lot of debate on that legislation, i.e., its validity. But I would leave that to a constitutional or legal expert to comment an opinion on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Theunens. I can agree with you in part. After all, it is a piece of legislation on defence, and you, as a military expert, should have more extensive knowledge about it than me, and I mean in relation to this particular field. I am not calling into question your knowledge and expertise, the vast knowledge and expertise you have. Can we have Articles 15 and 23 of the law. That's on the following page. Where, in my view, and I'm suggesting it to you, a point which was envisaged under the SFRY law of 1982 is being specified. So look at Article 15 which reads: "Organising and preparing citizens for armed struggle and other forms of armed resistance shall be carried out by the -- shall be carried out within units and institutions of the Army of Yugoslavia and units and organs of home affairs." So do you agree that at least under this particular law, which says so explicitly, did these competent organs have the power to prepare citizens and engage in other forms of activities aimed at preparing armed defence?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what Article 15 states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, I see that many in this courtroom are struggling with the connection with the server.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am informed that the server will be restarted and that we'll have access again within a couple of minutes. I suggest that we continue for the time being, looking at our left screens where the text is still scrolling. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I have only one question left on the issue of legislation, and that's in relation to Article 23. I'd like to hear your interpretation of the article. It reads: "All citizens, according to their abilities and understand conditions as provided in Article 22, paragraphs 2 and 3 of the present law, shall have the right and duty to be trained for defence of the country. "The federal government shall issue rules regulating the training of citizens for the defence of the countries as stipulated in paragraph 1 of this Article." Mr. Theunens, according to this law, was the federal government the one which issued rules and regulations for the purposes of training citizens as provided in Article -- in paragraph 1 of this article?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Article 23 states that it is the federal government that shall issue rules regulates the training of citizens for the defence of the country as stipulated in the first paragraph of that article.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. I needed to ask you this because it will form the basis for my further submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have a look at 2D306 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would object to using this document at this time. It's one of the documents for which the Prosecution has not received a translation to before court. We also received, right before court, an indication of the order, from the Simatovic Defence, of exhibits, and I see this one was not appearing in the -- the order that we were provided. So we haven't even -- I believe that there are some translations that just recently became available, but, of course, in my reviewing of what was noticed to us to -- even recently, in terms of how to prioritise it, this document wasn't included in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, has any translation been provided?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we did include it, and my learned friend is right when he said that we did it today. It is possible, perhaps, that inadvertently an error was made in the order. But perhaps we could have a look at the document with the witness now and then at the end of this process I will be tendering these documents, so Mr. Weber will have time enough to review the document and make his objections, if any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, time enough. At least additional time. Mr. Weber, let's have a look at the document. We do not know yet what it is. It could be a one-line document. I've got no idea. So before we say yes or no, wouldn't it be good to have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we're objecting. Mr. Bakrac is going to have a day and a half -- well, today and tomorrow. We're asking for, at the very least, an opportunity to know what the document is that's being shown to the witness, which, I guess, is now - since I'm seeing the translation for the first time ever - from the federal Ministry of Justice and is just not a one-page -- of a one-line document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The last thing, I can confirm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, would it disturb your flow of evidence to be presented if we would look at it tomorrow or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I only wanted to have continuity and to follow up on the laws relating to associations of citizens. But if it makes matters easier for the Prosecutor, I will go back to this document tomorrow. But just to summarize: It's a decision whereby the Serbian Guard was entered in the register of social and political organisations. The decision was issued by the Ministry of Justice, and the statement of reasons indicates that there was an earlier decision under the old law. In item 4, it is stated that a similar decision dating back to January 1991 was hereby made null and void.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, Mr. Bakrac was kind enough to already inform you briefly about what you could expect in the document which he will deal with tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We're not looking to have any discussions about the document. There are a substantial number of documents that we don't have translations to. If we could have an opportunity to look at them and then reserve any position for tomorrow, when we look at [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're already anticipating on what will follow. This document Mr. Bakrac will deal with tomorrow. Please proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will proceed. Can we have now D118, please. It's an admitted document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, did you have occasion to review the document at -- over the weekend? I'm -- I apologise. We don't have it on our screens yet, so I'm sure you can't even answer it. We'll wait for you to have a look at it. You have it before you now, Mr. Theunens. Did you have occasion to go through it over the weekend?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went through the CD I received from you. I don't remember whether this document was on the CD, but I may have missed it. But, anyway, I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. If you look at the last paragraph in B/C/S, and it's also the last paragraph in English, please read through. This is a letter by Dusan Smiljanic, a colonel or assistant commander for security intelligence of the Main Staff of the Serbian Army of Krajina. Did you know that on the 15th of October, 1994, this particular individual held this position?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You say 1994 or 1993? Because the document states 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I see that the document states the date when this was written and when Colonel Dusan Smiljanic qualified himself as assistant commander for security and intelligence of the Main Staff of the Serb army of the Krajina. So it's the 15th of October, 1994. Since you were involved in military affairs in this case, my question to you is whether you can confirm that this person was in actual fact assistant commander for security in the Main Staff of the Army of the Republic of the Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Colonel Dusan Smiljanic was a security organ in the SVK. Now, I have no reason to doubt what you're stating. I'm more familiar with his successor, even though I don't remember his exact name at this stage. But I know that lieutenant-colonel -- or Colonel - excuse me - Smiljanic was at the senior level in the security organs of the SVK at the time you mentioned, October 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Theunens, if we look at -- actually, can we go back to the first page now. I would briefly like to jog your memory in terms of the substance of this letter. The letter is being sent to General Ratko Mladic to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska, and Mr. Smiljanic is looking back at everything that had happened in the area of the Krajina. At the end of the first paragraph, he refers to what happened in Plitvice in March 1991, and he says that he was sent to Plitvice at his personal request together with a group of officers, that he remained in the area of the republic of the Serb Krajina until July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please move on to page 2 now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now the second paragraph, where he specifically states that he is illegally linking up with the key people of the Serb democratic people from the area of Lika, Banija, Kordun, and Banja Luka, and with a group of security organs and VP - I assume that VP is military post code - on -- at the end of April and the beginning of May. I starts arming the Serb people illegally from the arms depots that were in Otocac, Sveti Rok, and Skradin, and that in that -- at that point in time in July 1991 various infantry weapons and mortars were distributed in this ways, as well as guns and large amounts of ammunition, in this area of Lika, Kordun, and Banja. You have seen this document. My question is: Why is it not contained in your report? Because I think that it provides some important figures about the ways in which the Serb people were armed in the republic of the Serb Krajina.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: First just a small correction: The VP stands for "vojna policija" here, so for military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, sorry.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem. It is correct that I have not included this document in my report for the reason that I -- I tried to focus in this report on the role of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia. So I didn't conduct a detailed analysis of how Serbs in Croatia were armed, but I tried to focus and I tried to limited myself, as is indicated in the scope of the report, to any role played by the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia. And I think -- I mean, just to be complete --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be complete, I think when your colleague asked questions about the arming of the -- of Serbs in Croatia, I mentioned the role of the JNA, as well as of -- as well as of other organisations as we discussed over the last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, wasn't it relevant for you to include in your report this particular fact? I'm going to ask you now, because you were dealing with the Serbian MUP and the assistance that it had provided to the Krajina, do you have any idea of the type and amount of equipment that was provided by the Serb MUP to the Republic of Krajina?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The documents I reviewed do not provide a detailed breakdown of the types and -- and numbers or amount of equipment that was provided by the MUP the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, with all due respect, and bearing in mind the fact that you had before you this fact, and a certain amount of assistance provided by the MUP of Serbia, wasn't it fair to include this document in your report so that it would be more correct and more realistic at that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could have included this document for the sake of being complete but then I would have to do -- would have to have included also a detailed breakdown of other assistance -- I mean, other JNA documents that refer to the provision of weapons. But it's -- I mean, yeah, I could have included it for the sake of completeness, but it doesn't change what I have put in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Theunens. Tell me -- before we move on to the second paragraph that has to do with the second part of your report, or, rather, the third part of your report, tell me: 15.000 pieces of different infantry weapons, according to military doctrine, how many brigades can be armed with that amount of equipment?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say it depends on the type of weapons. Because in some cases one soldier can have several weapons. But you would talk about several brigades. Four, five, six, depending on the nature of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Theunens. Please look at the next paragraph now. This same Colonel at the time, from the security organs - and we did deal with many alleged documents of the security service. And now there's a reference to the territory of Bosnia, and it says that in July 1991 he went to the area of Novi Grad in Banja Luka where he linked up with Stojan Zupljanin, Brdjanin, and some other persons. And that during the course of that month he organised, again, the provision of over 20.000 various pieces of weapons from the arms depot in Skradnik, to Celinac and Drvar. This equipment included mortars, bombs, Zoljas, and two BKs and I believe that these are two combat sets of ammunitions or kits. Is this a fact that did you not deem relevant when you were compiling your report?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours, I have answered the question. I could have included this document if I wanted to address in detail the role of the JNA in arming local Serb military structures in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would also like to emphasise that this is a personal letter. It is not an official document. So -- and as I mentioned earlier, I could have included this for the sake of completeness, but I haven't done so. And I did --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Mr. Theunens, you said a few moments ago that you had no reason to doubt this document, that you knew this Mr. Smiljanic. And now it seems to me that you are trying to bring into question the authenticity of the document. Or am I wrong perhaps?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood the observation to be that it was a authentic but not formal document, a personal letter on matters which could have reported in a formal sense in the existing hierarchy, whereas this is a more personal nature. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour, I do apologise. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Now, do you have any reason to doubt the substance of what Mr. Smiljanic wrote to General Ratko Mladic in this document, in this letter?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know overall that there was -- there is information indicating the participation of security organs in, say, summer and -- and fall 1991, in providing assistance, equipment to local Serb defence structures in -- in Banja, Kordun, and maybe also Lika, so the area that was covered by Sector North in the time when UNPROFOR was deployed. But I haven't seen any official documents on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, for the sake of clarity, I do not share your position that this is a private document. Please look at the last page. This document was officially registered in the Main Staff at the Security Department of the Army of the Republic of the Serb Krajina on the 16th of October, 1994. So that is one matter. And now there's another matter: I did not understand you quite well, I assume. It was my understanding that you were a military expert in this case, and it was the activity of the army that you dealt with in the area concerned, and also at the time that is relevant to this document. In -- or, rather, you were not dealing with the indictment in that way; you were just investigating the activities of the MUP, or, rather, explaining that. Are you a military expert here? Am I wrong about the capacity in which you appear here?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just -- to make sure that -- that what I wanted to state is correctly effected, I want to emphasise that in page 26, line 15, I needed to have said the security organs of the JNA. Now to come back to your question. Indeed, there a stamp on the document, but that is just, in my view, reflects that the document has been officially registered but the contents still remains the same. It is a personal letter by Colonel Smiljanic to General Mladic. Why he had it registered to as -- as such, we should ask Smiljanic. Now to answer the second part of your question. The scope of the report is very clear. I tried to focus on the military aspects of the role of the Ministry of Interior of the Republic of Serbia in this report. It is obviously not an overall analysis of, for example, in this specific discussion, how the Serbs in -- how Serbs in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina were armed, how they created their own defence or military structures, and so on. That would go beyond the scope of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, but you will agree with me that you your report would have been a lot more realistic and a lot more complete and complex and that it would reflect far more faithfully the role of the MUP in these developments had you taken into account these facts which I deem very important; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I think, Mr. Bakrac, you've now tried six, seven, or eight times to illustrate for us that what others did may be relevant, if you are assessing what the MUP did. Now, that was clear to me 15 minutes ago. If you want to spend another 15 minutes on it, but it's your time. It's -- it's -- it's clear that Mr. Theunens says, I focussed on documents directly relating to the MUP. And you said it would have shed light if you would have also paid attention to documents which -- which more or less explains the developments but which were focussing on activity of other organisations. Therefore, I leave it to you. But I would suggest that you move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Your Honour, I'm grateful. I understand, and I shall move on. But I just have one question left.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I think that I counted this right. You included in your report 19 different articles or books or interviews of Vojislav Seselj. It seems that this was more important for you than documents that are fact-based and that come from security organs. We will also go back to another thing that you made comments, with regard to some unsigned reports of security organs, that in this way, or some other way, gave a bad impression of the security service.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the question is.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: My question is: Do you do not think -- or, rather, do you think that newspaper articles of a political leader at the time who, inter alia, wrote other books, also since he came here to the Tribunal, are they more important than a signed document, a registered document, which is evidence provided by a military person in an area that you had dealt with?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, we have been a few times over this. It is all a matter of first looking at the scope of the report which has been explained actually in introduction to report. And then, next, of the second aspect of my answer, is the methodology that is applied. And obviously one considers a wide range of written documentation when one compiles such a report, and some of this written documentation can consist of open-source material, including personal statements of senior politicians, and so on. So -- and sometimes documents are unsigned that -- and that has also been highlighted in the report. Just to finish my answer, I think it's also important to realise, that we're -- I mean, there's report, discussions, and activity which was, to say the least, hidden to the -- to the public for obvious reasons. As you know, the United Nations imposed sanctions, I mean, economic sanctions, against FRY in May 1992 as a punishment, between brackets, for the -- what was considered the continuous involvement of the FRY in the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and provisional support and so on. And the subject matter that is discussed in the report directly concerns this kind of support by one branch of the authorities of the Republic of Serbia. So I wouldn't say that it is a surprise that there's so little documentation and even that some of the documentation is unsigned.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm looking at the clock. Perhaps this would be a convenient moment for the break, if you so allow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is, Mr. Bakrac. We'll have a break, and we will resume at 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, before I show you a document, I'd like to ask you this: Do you know General Tumanov?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was a general in the JNA. He was of Macedonian ethnicity. And I believe that in the first half of 1992, or at least until April or May, he was the deputy chief of the security administration of the SFRY armed forces.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I proceed, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, when we now say -- actually, you said what the area of responsibility of the 2nd Military District is. In the situation when a state of imminent threat of war was declared, or a state of war, what are the duties and responsibilities of the military organs and the security organs in the area of the military district? The military security organs; that is what the interpretation should say. So, we saw what the situation was. A state of imminent threat of war was declared. There is the area of responsibility of the 2nd Military District. I would be interested in the rights and responsibilities of the military organs and the security organs in their area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to answer that question because I have not seen a specific document, or documents, that describe these rights and responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I fully understand what you're saying. I would now be interested in the following: In a military doctrine, could you tell us what the rights and responsibilities of the military authorities would be in that kind of a situation? My question before that was whether you read the Law on the Army and the rules of conduct, in order to be able to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure with -- with the rules -- I mean, which specific rules of conduct you are hinting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: In the JNA. As a military expert, did you have access to the rules of service? It's called the rules of service in the JNA. As a military expert who dealt with military matters, did you explore and study that? That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know of a 1985 Law on the Service in the Armed Forces, but I don't remember, at this stage, whether there were specific duties or rights identified in that law in relation to military organs during one of the three states.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Can you give us an example from a military, doctrinary point of view. If a state of war is declared or an imminent state of war is declared, what are the rights and responsibilities of military security organs and military authorities in their area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I cannot answer the question because I don't remember seeing such a document for the SFRY armed forces or the JNA. There is one document I managed to identify, which I mentioned -- I mean, I mentioned it earlier, from the -- I think the SFRY armed forces Supreme Command Staff, which is from early October 1992, and specifically highlights the situation with volunteers, i.e., emphasizing the importance of volunteers to reinforce the manpower of the JNA. But I'm not able to answer your question further.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, with all due respect, as an expert who was given the task of compiling a military analysis in a particular area, were you not interested in taking into account all relevant military legislation, all military rules? That is a basic document, the rules of service in the JNA. Quite simply, I'm surprised now. Is it possible that when you wrote up your report you were not interested in that, to see what this basic document says?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether you're accurately representing my previous answer. I explicitly made reference to the 1985 Law on the Service in the Armed Forces. Again, if there is another regulation I haven't seen, well, please show it to me and then show me the relevant passages so I can comment on them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, first of all, the rules you were referring to, are those the same as the law Mr. Theunens referred to? I mean, is there any disagreement in that respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, perhaps I'm not understanding you fully. The rules I'm referring to are not those laws on defence. Those are the rules of service in the JNA. I shall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... line 17, page 40, you say: "It's called the rules of service in the JNA." So you had a certain set of rules on your mind. Mr. Theunens started his answer by saying: "I know of a 1985 Law of the Service in the Armed Forces, but I don't remember, at this stage ..." So let's first establish whether had you a different set of rules on your mind as the ones Mr. Theunens referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that this is called the rules of service in the JNA. It is not -- it is not a law on service in the JNA. This is the basic document that regulates --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. When was that document issued? Do you have a copy of it so that we can look at it? We are having a debate, and you are proclaiming Mr. Theunens for not considering a certain piece of legislation or rules or whatever, when we have not even established whether we are talking about the same set of rules. Your rules of service in the JNA were issued when?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do apologise. I've been taken by surprise. I thought that Mr. Theunens had taken that into account. I am referring to the rules of service --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yes, but, there's no need to express now for the third or the fourth time your surprise. I'm just trying to get you both on the same track. That's the only thing I'm doing at this moment. Your set of rules, the rules of service in the JNA, were issued when and by whom?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Issued by the Federal Assembly in 1985, and I think that Mr. Theunens mentioned that. Could he, on the basis of that, explain to us what the areas of responsibility of a brigade is and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- so we now establish more or less that you are -- you say it's no law but it's of 1985 and issued by the -- by the Federal Assembly and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. Let me be very specific. The document is actually sponsored by the Ministry of Defence and ultimately passed by the Ministry of Defence but is approved by the Federal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. It's still not perfectly clear whether we're talking about the same document. I would say there's an 80 or 90 per cent chance that we do, but it's still not finally established. Now, what you asked Mr. Theunens, when he referred to what he considered to be part of your question, he referred to this -- what he called the Law of 1985, and you asked him whether he could give an example. He said something about that law, and then he said, But I can't further answer your question at this moment. Which means that he can't give an example by the top of his head of any of the elements you asked for. So there we are. We are talking about the same document. Mr. Theunens has not a recollection which allows him to give an example as you asked him. And that's where we are. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, on page 41 of today's transcript I see, in conjunction with this discussion, Mr. Bakrac asked: "What are the right and responsibilities of military security organs and military authorities in their area of responsibility?" I just -- in order to avoid any confusion, I do not know if Mr. Bakrac is referring to P1036 which are the rules of service of the security organs in the SFRY armed forces. So I just bring this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- bring this up to see if this is the same document that Mr. Bakrac is referring to or a different one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1046 you said?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: 1036. I see that it is published in 1984.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then most likely it's not the same. Different year, different title. Mr. Theunens, I just wanted to establish where we were at that time. Not a full 100 per cent certainty that we're talking about the same. You asked for examples, Mr. Theunens is -- said something about the document he is aware of and couldn't give any examples. Next question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If you allow me, Your Honours, actually the law on the service in the armed forces, "zakon o sluzbi o oruzanim snagama," is -- from 1985, is P1012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If that can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is that the one you were hinting at, Mr. Bakrac? Then we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your leave, I'm going to skip this question. I'm going to look into it again, and perhaps I shall go back to it later. I would just like to check this. I hadn't printed this because I didn't think that there was any need to cite anything from there, but if you allow me, I'm going to skip the question for the time being and go back to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you ask a specific question about a document, then at least you should be aware of what that document is, isn't it? Especially if it's in evidence. Because that makes life easier if we know what we are talking about. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, when my learned friend Mr. Jordash was cross-examining you, if I understood things correctly, you said, when speaking about the Serb Radical Party and the volunteers of the Serb Radical Party, that it seemed to you that after November 1993 the MUP started bringing pressure on the Serb Radical Party. Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you're paraphrasing a bit, but what I was trying to explain is that only after there is a political fallout or break between Mr. Milosevic, president of Serbia at the time, and Mr. Seselj, president of the Serbian Radical Party, that only at that time the competent authorities in the Republic of Serbia, including the MUP, start to act against, in particular, senior SRS volunteers. And I've seen a number of documents indicating that these senior SRS volunteers are then arrested on the basis of charges for the illegal possession of weapons. And, again, these are just a number of documents. I haven't analysed the whole issue in detail, and I cannot provide any statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, I think that I did paraphrase you correctly, and I think that we can agree that you were referring to the period from the second half of 1993 onwards, that that's when that happened; right?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I have a recollection of November. But we would have to look at the specific documents in order to ascertain when this starts. Or to establish, I'm sorry, to establish when this exactly starts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would -- I would now like to ask that we move into private session because I would like to put something to Mr. Theunens that is actually the transcript of a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, indeed, conclude in the report that the Serbian Volunteer Guard, on the basis of the documents I reviewed, during combat operations operated under JNA command. There are also documents from the 1st Military District, security organs, indicating that outside combat operations the Serbian Volunteer Guard conducted other activities, including criminal activities, whereby they were not -- at least on the basis of these documents, not subordinated to the JNA. As a second aspect of my answer: On the basis of the document, I concluded that the Serbian minister of interior controlled or maintained other relations with groups like the Serbian Volunteer Guard. I couldn't find a specific -- or I couldn't, yeah, find a specific military definition for the type of relation, but at least on the basis of the documents I could conclude that the Serbian minister of interior allowed the Serbian Volunteer Guard to exist from at least fall 1991 to September 1995 without interfering with its activities, even though there was public knowledge or even information available to the Serbian authorities that members of the Serbian Volunteer Guard, including Arkan, had allegedly been involved in serious crimes. There're also examples -- I mean, obviously when you look at the map, the Serbian authorities, including the MUP, allowed the Serbian Volunteer Guard to transit from Serbia towards Eastern Slavonia, to remove certain goods from Eastern Slavonia. One famous example, it's not the Serbian Volunteer Guard itself but it's the -- are the Skorpions located at the Dzeletovci oil --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Sir, witness, all this is contained in your report, and there's no need for you to repeat it. I will now show you some exhibits and we'll see if perhaps they'll change your mind. My intention was to show you, tomorrow, a document whereby the Ministry of Justice registered the Serbian Guard as a socio-political organisation. Did you know that Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, was a deputy in the Serbian Assembly sometime from mid-1992?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed, I know. And on the basis of the information that was already available at the time in relation to alleged criminal activities by Mr. Zeljko Raznjatovic in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, one could consider quite remarkable, but it's not something I have analysed in the scope of -- in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, if I were to tell you an assumption - and we'll see what the evidence will show - that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was registered as a socio-political organisation or social organisation by the Ministry of Justice, and if we proceed from the assumption that the testimony of Witness JF-047 on the issue of MUP of Serbia's attitude toward volunteers was true, was there a reason for the MUP of Serbia to arrest Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and members of his guard?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a bit confused by the first part of your question because are you now stating that the Serbian Volunteer Guard, also known as the Arakanovci, were registered as a socio-political organisation? Or are you referring to the document on a Serbian Guard, "Srpska Garda," that we saw briefly on the screen earlier today?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, no. My question was a hypothetical one. Had the Serbian Volunteer Guard been registered in the register of socio-political organisations as was the Serbian Guard, would there have existed a basis for its members to be arrested if they had not committed a crime in the territory of the Republic of Serbia if they had not milled about Serbia carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, that's a legal question and it's outside the scope of my report. Because one would have to establish first what are the legal criteria in order to be registered as a socio-political organisation, and which activities prevent -- for example, which activities prevents an organisation from being registered as a socio-political organisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, your question was, to that extent, a bit confusing, that you started by saying: "If I were to tell you an assumption - and we'll see what the evidence will show ..." which means it's an assumption, but, at the same time, we should take it for a fact that the Serbian Volunteer Guard was registered, and, if, as you said, we proceed from the assumption that the witness -- so therefore the second assumption is included in the question that -- on the issue of the MUP Serbia attitude towards volunteers was true. So we have two assumptions. One being translated more into a expectation of being established, and then I'm not surprised that Mr. Theunens is a bit confused as well. Apparently what you want to ask him - at least that's how I understand it to be: If an organisation is registered as a socio-political organisation, would there be any reason to arrest members of it apart from if there's a reasonable suspicion that they committed offences. Is that what you wanted to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's what I wanted to ask. So to keep matters short, that's what I wanted to ask. And I -- my question was to be placed in the context of the Republic of Serbia, because I'm asking about the MUP of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, have you, meanwhile, understood the question, Mr. Theunens, to be looked at in the MUP of Serbia context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, I -- I remain convinced it's a legal question, but I would address this from a common sense point of view, whether or not somebody is a member of a socio-political organisation is not a -- kind of an exonerating factor or has any other impact in case of criminal behaviour. Everybody should be equal to the law. And if a socio-political organisation starts to undertake or plan activities - I refer now to Article 118 of the Law on Defence - or other criminal activities, then I would expect that the organisation would be investigated and that the law would be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Theunens. I agree with you fully. But if a member committed a crime outside the territory of the Republic of Serbia and there is no evidence about that crime, do you think that there is room for MUP to react to that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is, again, a legal question which is outside the scope of my report. But --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bakrac, I suggest to you that we do not ask Mr. Theunens to answer that question, because if a crime is committed outside of the territory, this raises a whole textbook of theories on continuing crimes, crimes of which elements are committed within the territory but other parts outside the territory, the principle of ubiquity ... this covers -- I could easily write a hundred pages on that, just to describe the difficulties in saying what is a crime committed within and what is a crime committed outside. So, therefore, Mr. Theunens, I don't think you could write that book, or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You couldn't write that book. Now that, of course, might be of great importance for the MUP to react yes or no. And then we have the applicability of substantive law. And then we have procedural law, to what extent can enforcement agencies act outside the scope or only inside the scope of the territory. It's a rather complex legal question, which is very intriguing. But I don't think, as a matter of fact, that on the present circumstances, n the basis of the evidence that we have now, that we should ask Mr. Theunens about it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I fully agree with you. Perhaps I'm not conducting my examination appropriately, but I'd like to draw Their Honours' attention to the fact that there is not enough basis in the report to draw that conclusion. Let me ask Mr. Theunens the following question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... isn't it true that Mr. Jordash has extensively questioned the witness about whether they could react, if we're talking about offences which are committed outside the territory of the Republic of Serbia? Mr. Jordash, I'm not inventing things, am I? That was part of your cross-examination, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. JORDASH
utterances.text: Yes, I covered some of that. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, quite extensively, I do remember. So, Mr. Bakrac, if you want to draw our attention to something Mr. Jordash has already drawn our attention to, then it's your time, and -- but it is repetitious.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... there's any new element in it, then please focus your questions on the new element.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I agree. Thank you. Since our time for the break is nearing, I'd like to ask Mr. Theunens to tell me how many documents did he come across where the security organ within whose area of responsibility the alleged crimes were committed by Arkan, how many such documents were there where the MUP was informed and provided sufficient documentation in order to take any steps? And I'm sure Mr. Theunens will have an opportunity to give us an answer to that after the break. How extensively were they able to prosecute, given the area of their responsibility, given -- and I'm talking about the security organs.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Mr. Bakrac please repeat the document number he's asking for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the document number you were --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2D64. Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, we don't have the English translation yet. Mr. Theunens, this is a certificate signed by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and JNA colonel Enes Taso, confirming that Nenad Markovic of Belgrade was a member of a unit which acted in coordinated action with the JNA. And we're coming to this issue where you said that the Arkan's Men were under JNA command when participating in combat activities. And I'm referring you to D63 where we can see that in the battle at Luzac, Arkan was subordinated or under the command of the JNA Colonel Enes Taso. You do remember this document, Mr. Theunens, don't you?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, I mean, from somewhere this combat operation or this attack, but I don't remember seeing D63. Maybe I did and it's my fault, but I don't remember. D63.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: 2D63. But I'll not waste any time on this because you do not dispute the fact that in combat activities they acted thus. So please look first look at the stamp and the heading and tell me if you agree that the special training centre at Erdut, judging by the stamp and the heading, was a training centre belonging to the Territorial Defence of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment in time, indeed. So on the 4th of December, 1991, the training centre in Erdut is identified as centre for special training of the TO of -- the self-established TO of SBWS.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Yes, sir --

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but -- I mean, looking at the stamps, at the same time, there is a stamp which states "command of the volunteer training centre." Maybe it's an old stamp. Because I know that the training centre in Erdut changed a few times of names. Later, sometime in 1993, Arkan withdrew for some months but then he came back and again the name changed a few times, but the link with Arkan remained the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, could I ask you one question. When you summarized the document, you suggested, I think, that Arkan's Men were under JNA command and that at the "battle of Luzac, Arkan was subordinated or under the command of the JNA ..." Is that what you read in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I had wanted to follow some of your previous instructions. When there is no coalition, we should try to avoid a waste of time. I can actually ask for 2D63 to be called up, and the battle of Luzac, and you will see that it is under the command of Enes Taso and the 52nd Brigade, that we can see Arkan and his men. 2D63. Perhaps we can call that up and you'll see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because in this document, which is on our screen now, it says "cooperation with the JNA" and no subordination. I just wanted to have this clarified. If you say we can read it differently in 2D63, I'll do that. And there's no need to have it on the screen at this moment, unless you would insist. I'm looking at the clock. I'd like, first of all, to have Mr. Theunens to already take his break. He has two questions on his piece of paper, I take it. Mr. Theunens, if you would be kind enough to consider those questions. And then I would have one further matter to briefly raise with you, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the usher escort Mr. Theunens out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac, I'm just trying to follow the line, to follow the thoughts behind your questions and try to verify whether I understand the evidence you're eliciting. One of the issues that you apparently want to raise is that if this witness says that on from, I think, it was November 1993 when there was a clash between Seselj and Milosevic, that it was only then that they started arresting people, as the witness said, that he's wrong because on the basis of the other evidence it is shown that, already in 1991, people could not carry weapons in the bus because they might be stopped. And did I understand you well that that is an issue you raised?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying to reconcile this with another issue which apparently was raised this morning on a more legislative level, that is, that everyone had the right to defend himself and to form groups and to do all that. So I'm trying to reconcile, why, on the one hand, you say it was not only in 1993 but already in 1991 that the MUP took action against volunteers.
